title: How to Clean Up Startup Apps for a Faster Boot (and Keep It That Way)
desc: A decision rule for which startup items to disable, how to measure the difference, and what to leave alone.
text: How-to How to Clean Up Startup Apps for a Faster Boot (and Keep It That Way) 2026-10-11 · sabaoongfx · 2 min read Every program that launches at login competes for the same CPU, disk and memory while you wait for your desktop. Over a year of installing software, startup lists grow quietly. Cleaning them up is one of the safest, highest-value speed improvements available, and it costs nothing. Why startup items pile up Many installers add themselves to startup by default: chat apps, cloud-sync clients, game launchers, update helpers, printer utilities, hardware tool suites. Each is reasonable alone. Together they can add minutes to boot and hundreds of megabytes of resident memory that you never asked for. A decision rule For each item on the startup list, ask three questions: Do I need it within the first minute? A password manager, maybe. A game launcher, almost never. Does it need to be running to do its job? A sync client must run to sync. A tool you open by hand doesn’t. Do I know what it is? If not, search before touching it. Keep items that answer “yes” to the first two. Disable the rest. Disabling a startup entry doesn’t uninstall anything; the program still works, it just won’t launch itself. What to leave alone Security software that protects you from the first second. Drivers and system helpers for your touchpad, audio or display. Disabling them can break hardware features. Anything you don’t recognise and can’t identify. Leave it until you know. Measure before and after Don’t trust the feeling of speed. Restart, wait until the desktop is fully usable and the disk quiets down, then open the Performance view and record memory in use and CPU. Make your changes, restart again, and compare. A few hundred megabytes is a typical saving. The Processes tab, sorted by memory or CPU right after login, shows exactly which startup programs are the heaviest. What Open Task Manager does here The Startup apps tab lists the programs configured to launch at login. On Linux it reads real autostart entries from your system. Be aware of the current limitation: toggling Enable or Disable updates the interface but does not yet change the real entry, and on Windows and macOS the list is not populated in the installed app. These gaps are on the roadmap . Until they are closed, use your desktop’s own settings to make the change: Task Manager’s Startup tab on Windows, Login Items on macOS, or your desktop environment’s autostart settings on Linux. Then use Open Task Manager to verify the effect. Keeping it clean When installing software, look for a “launch at startup” checkbox and clear it. Review the list every few months, or after installing something large. Remove programs you no longer use rather than just disabling them. The result is a machine that is ready sooner, with more memory left for the work you actually want to do ( more habits here ).

title: CPU Usage Explained: Cores, Threads and What That Percentage Means
desc: Why a program can show 400%, why 12% can mean a core is maxed, and how to tell a harmless spike from a real problem.
text: Fundamentals CPU Usage Explained: Cores, Threads and What That Percentage Means 2026-10-11 · sabaoongfx · 3 min read CPU percentage looks like the simplest number in a task manager. It is also one of the most misread. To use it well, you need three ideas: cores, threads and the thing the percentage is measured against. Cores and logical processors A modern processor has several cores , each able to run instructions independently. Many cores can also present themselves as two logical processors (simultaneous multithreading), so a six-core chip may appear as twelve. Your operating system schedules work across all of them. When a monitor says “100 percent,” the key question is: 100 percent of what? Two conventions Percent of the whole machine. 100 means every logical processor is saturated. A program fully using one core on a twelve-processor machine shows about 8 percent. The Windows Task Manager works this way for its main CPU figures since the 24H2 change, and so does Open Task Manager since version 0.4.2 ( the story ). Percent of one core. 100 means one core is fully used, and a multi-threaded program can exceed it: 400 means about four cores’ worth of work. Many Unix-style tools follow this convention. Open Task Manager did too until version 0.4.2, when we switched to the whole-machine share so process rows add up to the total at the top, as they do in Windows. Neither is wrong. They answer different questions: “how busy is the machine?” versus “how much of a core is this program consuming?” Always check which one your tool is using before comparing numbers. Single-threaded bottlenecks A program that uses only one thread can use at most one core. On a twelve-core machine that is about 8 percent overall, so the system looks nearly idle even though that program is as fast as it can possibly go and still feels slow. If a program is sluggish while the overall chart is low, look at its per-core or per-process figure. One core pinned at 100 percent is the clue. What “normal” looks like Spikes. Short bursts of 50 to 100 percent when you open something are expected. Idle. A resting desktop should hover in low single digits. Sustained load. Anything above about 30 percent for minutes, when you aren’t doing demanding work, deserves a look. Laptops add a wrinkle: speed changes constantly. A core at half speed running flat out reports as busy, so the same percentage can mean different amounts of work. Some tools adjust for this (Windows’s utility-style metric does) and others don’t. Finding the culprit Open the Processes tab and sort by CPU. Let it settle for ten seconds, since it jumps around. Identify the top entry and check whether it is an app you are using. If it is an unfamiliar helper, look it up. Indexing, backups, antivirus scans and updates all legitimately use CPU for a while. If it never settles, check the Performance tab for the overall pattern and restart the app, or see how to end a stuck process safely . Remember the refresh rate Every monitor samples at an interval; ours refreshes every 1.5 seconds. Percentages are averages over that window, so very short bursts can fall between samples. For tracking down intermittent problems, watch the chart for a minute rather than reading one instant. And if you see many more entries than expected, see process versus thread .

title: Disk at 100%? How to Diagnose a Slow Drive Step by Step
desc: The most frustrating slowdowns come from the disk, not the CPU. Learn to confirm it, find the cause, and decide whether you need new hardware.
text: How-to Disk at 100%? How to Diagnose a Slow Drive Step by Step 2026-10-11 · sabaoongfx · 3 min read Your computer is crawling, but the CPU chart is nearly flat and there is plenty of memory free. That pattern points to the storage drive. When a disk is saturated, everything that needs to read or write waits in line, and the whole machine feels frozen. It is a common problem on older laptops and machines with traditional hard drives. Confirm it is the disk Open the Performance view and look at the disk section. The key figure is active time : the percentage of time the drive was busy handling requests. Open Task Manager reports this from the operating system on Linux, using the kernel’s own disk counters, alongside read and write throughput. A reading pinned near 100 percent for a long stretch, with low throughput, means the drive is spending its time on lots of small operations instead of moving big files. That is the worst case, especially on hard drives. Low throughput with high active time is the signature of a hard drive seeking, or a nearly full or failing drive. High throughput with high active time just means a large copy is running, which is fine. Find the cause Sort the Processes tab by Disk. The top entry is usually the answer. Check the usual suspects: search indexers, antivirus scans, backup and sync clients, update installers, and software that has just been installed. Check memory. If RAM is full, the system swaps memory to disk and the drive thrashes. In that case the real problem is memory ( see why ). Check free space. Drives slow down when almost full, especially SSDs, which need spare room to manage writes. Find what is taking the space If the drive is nearly full, the quickest fix is finding what is using the room. Open Task Manager has a WinDirStat-style Disk usage tab that scans a folder and shows the result as a treemap, a tree, a list of the largest files, and a breakdown by file type. A treemap makes the culprit obvious: one oversized rectangle for a forgotten download folder, a video project or a cache directory. Check the folder before deleting, and don’t remove anything you can’t identify. What to do Pause the background job. Let the indexer or scan finish, or schedule it for the night. Free space. Aim to leave at least 15 to 20 percent of the drive free. Trim startup apps. Fewer things launching at login means fewer simultaneous disk reads ( guide ). Check drive health. A failing drive shows constant high activity and strange delays. Use the drive’s SMART data through your operating system’s tools, and back up first. Upgrade the drive. If you still use a hard drive as your system disk, moving to an SSD is the single biggest speed improvement available. With storage prices up this year ( more on that ), compare capacities carefully. When it is a false alarm A brief 100 percent right after boot is normal as the system loads. A long copy of a large file legitimately saturates the drive. Only worry when the pegged reading persists while you aren’t doing anything demanding. The habit to take away is to look at all four resources, CPU, memory, disk and network, before deciding what is wrong. A slow computer is rarely slow for the reason people first assume.

title: eBPF and the Future of Observability: Where a Desktop Monitor Fits
desc: eBPF lets programs watch the Linux kernel safely, and it is reshaping how servers are monitored. What it can do that a task manager can't, and the reverse.
text: Trends eBPF and the Future of Observability: Where a Desktop Monitor Fits 2026-10-11 · sabaoongfx · 3 min read If you follow infrastructure news, you have seen the term eBPF more and more. A recent industry study described it as reshaping categories from observability and network security to runtime security, cost management (FinOps), LLM observability and virtualised networking. That is a big claim for a kernel feature, and it is worth understanding what it is before deciding what it means for the humble task manager. What eBPF is eBPF lets you load small, verified programs into the Linux kernel that run when certain events happen: a system call, a network packet, a function being entered. The kernel checks each program for safety before running it, so it can’t crash the system the way a poorly written kernel module could. The programs can record what they see and hand it to tools in user space. The effect is a view into the system that previously required modifying the kernel or the application. Observability systems can capture detailed events at the kernel boundary without changing the software being watched. The same study describes this as especially useful for AI workloads, where teams want a detailed picture without extensive code changes. Vendors also position it as complementary to OpenTelemetry, which collects application-level data: eBPF fills in the kernel-to-application picture. What a task manager does differently A desktop or terminal monitor like Open Task Manager works on a much simpler model. Every 1.5 seconds it asks the operating system for a snapshot of processes, memory, disk and network counters, using the sysinfo library, and draws the result. On Linux that mostly means reading files under /proc . It does not install anything in the kernel, doesn’t need special privileges for the basics and doesn’t record continuously. eBPF-based tools Task manager Granularity Individual events (every call, packet) Samples every second or so Setup Needs kernel support and elevated privileges Run it; no setup Platform Linux (with growing efforts elsewhere) Linux, Windows, macOS Best for Production tracing, security, deep debugging Seeing what is using resources right now Learning curve Steep Minimal Why the simple tool still matters For most people, most of the time, the question is basic: what is using my CPU, and can I close it? Answering that needs a sample of current state, not a trace of every event. A tool that needs a kernel program and root access is the wrong shape for that job. The two layers complement each other, and a task manager is often the first step: it tells you which process to look at, then you reach for deeper tooling if the answer isn’t obvious. Where this is heading More depth, more safety. eBPF’s verifier model is a good example of getting power without sacrificing stability. Privacy implications. Tools that can see every event raise real questions about what they capture and who can read it. The principles in our piece on auditable software apply. Interfaces on top. Rich kernel data is only useful when someone can read it. Expect more friendly front ends. We are not planning to rebuild Open Task Manager around eBPF. Its job is to be simple, cross-platform and honest, and for that, polling is the right tool. We would welcome contributors who want to explore optional deeper data on Linux, though, and the project is open on GitHub .

title: Find the Apps Draining Your Laptop Battery
desc: A step-by-step way to track down background drains, what a task manager can and can't tell you about power, and the fixes that work.
text: How-to Find the Apps Draining Your Laptop Battery 2026-10-11 · sabaoongfx · 3 min read A laptop that used to last a full day now barely makes it to lunch. Battery drain is nearly always caused by software doing work you didn’t notice, and the work shows up in the same place as every other resource problem: your task manager. Power isn't measured directly there, but the things that burn it are. What actually uses power CPU activity. The processor is usually the biggest consumer. A busy core draws far more than an idle one, and constant small wake-ups prevent it from sleeping deeply. The screen. Often the single largest drain, and not something a process list shows. Disk and network. Wi-Fi radios and storage draw power while active, so chatty background syncing costs battery. The graphics chip. Video, animations and some web pages keep it awake. Because these are the causes, a task manager’s CPU, disk and network readings are good indirect indicators, even though they don’t show watts. The hunt Unplug and settle. Run on battery for a few minutes with your normal apps open and nothing demanding. Check the Performance tab. An idle laptop should sit at low single-digit CPU. If it hovers at 15 percent or higher while you do nothing, something is working. Sort the Processes tab by CPU. Watch for a minute. Ignore single spikes; look for something that keeps showing up near the top. Check disk and network. Sustained activity from a sync client, a backup or an updater drains power as well as bandwidth. Close or pause suspects one at a time. When the idle CPU drops, you have found a drain. The App history view, which accumulates CPU time per application since the app opened, is helpful here. Leave the monitor running for an hour while you work normally, then see which programs consumed the most processor time. Remember that it resets when the app restarts. Usual suspects Browsers with active tabs, especially video, ads or web apps that poll constantly. Cloud sync and backup clients indexing large folders. Search indexers after a big file change. Chat clients and other apps built on embedded browsers. Programs stuck in a busy loop after a crash. What a task manager can’t tell you Open Task Manager does not show energy use or battery data. For actual power attribution, use your platform’s own tools: Windows has a battery usage breakdown in Settings, macOS Activity Monitor has an Energy tab, and on Linux a tool called powertop estimates which programs and devices cause wake-ups. Use our monitor to find what is working, and those tools to see what it costs. Fixes that help Disable startup items you don’t need ( guide ). Close heavy browser tabs and extensions ( more here ). Lower screen brightness and refresh rate, which often beat any software tweak. Use your operating system’s battery saver mode, which limits background activity. Keep the system updated; some drain bugs are fixed by patches. Measure your idle baseline before and after each change so you know what worked. Small, verified wins add up to hours.

title: How to Check What an App Sends Over the Network (Without Taking Anyone's Word)
desc: A practical, tiered guide: from a quick look at open connections to a full packet capture. Works on Windows, macOS and Linux.
text: Privacy How to Check What an App Sends Over the Network (Without Taking Anyone's Word) 2026-10-11 · sabaoongfx · 3 min read Every app makes claims about privacy, and most of them are impossible for a normal person to verify. But you can look. Network behaviour is one of the few things about software that can be observed from the outside, and the basic checks take minutes. This guide goes from quick to thorough. We encourage you to use it on our app, too. Level 1: see open connections The fastest check is to list which programs have network connections right now. Windows. Open Resource Monitor (search for it) and look at the Network tab, which lists processes with network activity and the addresses they talk to. In a terminal, netstat -ano lists connections with the owning process ID, which you can match to the PID column in a task manager. Linux. ss -tupn lists TCP and UDP sockets with the process attached, and lsof -i does something similar. You may need elevated rights to see other users’ processes. macOS. lsof -i works there too, and the built-in nettop shows live per-process traffic. Start the app you want to test, wait a minute, and run the command. Search for its name or PID. If it has no connections while idle, that is a good sign. Note that a brief check can miss traffic that happens only at certain times. Level 2: watch over time Some apps send data only occasionally, such as an update check on launch or a daily ping. Watch the machine-wide graph in your task manager with the app running and everything else closed ( how to read it ). Then repeat the connection check at intervals. A firewall that prompts you the first time a program tries to connect out gives you a log of each attempt. Examples include the Windows firewall in advanced mode, Little Snitch or LuLu on macOS, and OpenSnitch on Linux. Level 3: capture the traffic For a definite answer, capture the packets. Wireshark runs on all three systems. Start a capture, launch the app, use it for a while, then filter by the app’s traffic. Even when contents are encrypted, you can see who it talks to (addresses and domain names from DNS lookups), how often and how much. Be aware that you are looking at metadata : with modern encryption you can see that a program sent 40 KB to an analytics domain without reading what it said. Capturing can expose your own sensitive traffic to anyone with access to the capture file, so do it on a quiet machine and delete the file afterwards. How to interpret what you see No traffic at all. The most believable result for a local tool. Check also during actions like opening links, which should hand off to your browser. Update checks. Usually acceptable if they are disclosed, infrequent and documented. Connections to ad, analytics or tracking domains. A red flag for a tool that has no reason to send usage data. Large upload. Worth understanding before you use the tool further. What this can't prove Observation shows what happened while you watched. A program could behave differently later, on another machine, or only when it detects it is being monitored. That is why source code matters alongside testing: reading or searching the code tells you what is possible, and testing tells you what is happening. For Open Task Manager, you can do both; our comparison post lists what the code does and doesn’t include. If you find something we have missed, please open an issue. Taking five minutes to look turns privacy from a promise into something you checked.

title: How to End a Stuck Process Safely: SIGTERM, SIGKILL and End Task
desc: The difference between asking a program to quit and forcing it, what each risks, and how to do it on Windows, Linux and macOS.
text: How-to How to End a Stuck Process Safely: SIGTERM, SIGKILL and End Task 2026-10-11 · sabaoongfx · 3 min read Every computer user meets a frozen program eventually. The window won’t respond, the spinner never stops, and closing it does nothing. Ending its process is the standard fix. Done right it is safe; done carelessly it can lose unsaved work or destabilise your session. Here is how to do it well. Ask first, force second There are two levels of ending a process, and the difference matters. A polite request. On Unix-like systems this is the SIGTERM signal. It tells the program “please shut down,” and a well-behaved program saves state, closes files and exits. Windows’s equivalent is closing the main window. A forced kill. SIGKILL on Unix, or forced termination on Windows. The operating system removes the process immediately, with no chance to clean up. It always works on a process you own, but unsaved data is lost, and temporary files may be left behind. The sensible order is to wait a minute (some programs are busy, not frozen), try to close the window normally, then ask politely, and only then force. In practice, Open Task Manager’s End task action is a forced kill of the selected process; it is the one real action on your system that the app performs, so use it knowingly. Steps in a task manager Find the right row. Use search to filter by name. If the app is grouped, expand it to see its helpers. Check the details. Confirm the name and that it is owned by you. The Details tab shows PID and user. Right-click and choose End task. In the terminal UI, select the row and use its kill prompt, which asks you to confirm. Confirm the result. The row should disappear on the next refresh. If it comes back immediately, something is restarting it; look at the Services and Startup tabs. Ending a whole app versus one helper Ending the main process of a grouped app usually closes the rest. Ending a single helper can make the app show an error page or restart that part. If an app is partly broken, such as one browser tab that has crashed, ending just that helper is a gentler fix. What not to end System processes. On Windows, entries running as System that you can’t identify; on Linux, systemd , your display server or session manager. Ending these can log you out or freeze the machine. Anything you don’t recognise. Search the name before acting. Processes with unsaved work. If you can, copy the content out first. The operating system will often refuse if you lack permission, such as ending another user’s process or a protected one. That refusal is a safety feature, not a bug. Don’t reach for administrator rights unless you understand why you need them. If it keeps getting stuck Repeated hangs deserve diagnosis, not repeated killing. Watch the process in the monitor first. Does it use a lot of CPU (a loop), steadily grow in memory ( a leak ), or sit at zero while the disk is busy ( a disk problem )? Update the software, disable add-ons, and note what you were doing when it froze. That detail is what a bug report needs. New to the vocabulary? Start with what a process is .

title: How to Find a Memory Leak With Just a Task Manager
desc: A step-by-step method to confirm whether a program is leaking memory, and what to do about it, without any developer tools.
text: How-to How to Find a Memory Leak With Just a Task Manager 2026-10-11 · sabaoongfx · 3 min read A memory leak is a program that keeps asking for memory and never gives it back. Left running, it grows until the system slows, other programs are killed, or the machine runs out. You don’t need a debugger to spot one. A task manager and a bit of patience are enough to tell a leak from normal behaviour. Leak or just busy? Memory use rising is not proof of a leak. A browser grows as you open pages. An editor grows as you open files. Caches deliberately fill up. The distinguishing feature of a leak is that memory keeps climbing when the workload isn’t changing and doesn’t come back down when the work is done. The method Pick a suspect. Sort the Processes tab by memory. Look for the process you suspect, usually something you leave open for days. Record a start value. Note its memory, and the time. Group by app so helpers add into one total. Hold the workload steady. Don’t open new files or pages. Let it idle or repeat one simple action. Check at intervals. Look again after ten minutes, an hour, a day. A steady upward slope with nothing changing is the signature. Test the reset. Close the work inside the program (the document, the tab). If memory doesn’t fall, that is more evidence. Then restart the program; if it drops to the baseline and begins climbing again, the leak is in that program. The Performance tab helps with the machine-wide picture. If total memory climbs in step with one process, you have found your suspect. Open Task Manager’s App history tab, which accumulates CPU time per app since launch, adds a second clue: a leaking program that is also spinning will stand out. Common false alarms Caching. Programs that cache aggressively look like leaks until they hit their cap. Watch for a plateau. Garbage-collected runtimes. Languages that clean up periodically show a sawtooth: climb, drop, climb. That is normal; a rising baseline across the drops is not. Shared pages. Resident memory counts shared libraries. A jump when another program loads the same library isn’t a leak (see memory explained ). What to do once you’re sure Update. Leaks are common bugs and often fixed in newer releases. Check the changelog. Disable extensions or plugins. In browsers and editors, extensions are a frequent cause. Disable them one at a time and repeat the test. Work around it. Restart the program on a schedule, or on a lightly used machine, when it passes a threshold. Report it. Include your operating system, version, and the numbers from your test. A reproducible report with a slope and time is far more useful than “it uses too much RAM.” Be careful about ending the wrong thing If the leaking program is something you started, restarting it is safe. If it is a system process, don’t force-end it; restart the machine and report the issue. Our guide to ending processes safely covers the difference between asking a program to quit and forcing it. The method works in any task manager. It’s slow, but it separates real defects from ordinary growth, and that saves you from chasing the wrong program.

title: How We Built Open Task Manager: One Rust Core, Two Interfaces
desc: A behind-the-scenes look at the architecture: a shared data core, a Tauri desktop app, a terminal UI, a mock-data path, and a few deliberate shortcuts.
text: Engineering How We Built Open Task Manager: One Rust Core, Two Interfaces 2026-10-11 · sabaoongfx · 3 min read Open Task Manager looks like a single app, but it is really three pieces that share one engine. This post explains how they fit together and why we made the choices we did. Some are standard practice and some are deliberate compromises, and we'll flag which is which. A workspace with one core The project is a Cargo workspace with three crates: core/ ( otm-core ). All data collection lives here. A Monitor struct owns the sysinfo handles and the state needed to compute rates, such as disk throughput and the running CPU time per app. Its snapshot() returns everything the interface needs in one go. It also holds the code for the Services and Startup apps tabs, the disk scanner, and the types that are sent to the interface. src-tauri/ . The desktop shell. It is mostly thin command wrappers around the core, with the monitor held in shared state behind a lock. tui/ ( otm ). The terminal UI, built with ratatui and crossterm, which calls the same core functions directly. The rule we follow is: put new backend logic in the core, then expose it from both front ends. That keeps the desktop and terminal versions from drifting apart, and it makes the Rust code the single place where operating-system data is read. One poll loop On the desktop side, a single timer calls get_snapshot every 1.5 seconds. The result feeds the Processes, Performance and App history views as props. Tabs whose data doesn’t change quickly, namely Startup apps and Services, fetch once when they open. A single poll keeps the numbers consistent across tabs and means the OS is queried once per tick instead of once per component. The mock path Every data call in the interface branches on whether it is running inside Tauri. In a plain browser there is no backend, so the same components read generated data from a mock module instead. This has three payoffs: the frontend runs with npm run dev without a Rust toolchain, the end-to-end tests run against predictable data, and the live demo on our website is the real interface running on sample data rather than a mockup. The cost is discipline: every new backend feature needs a matching mock, or the tab will work in the real app and break in the browser. Deliberate duplication You will find the same table styling and right-click-menu code repeated across several tabs. That is intentional. With only a few such tabs, a shared abstraction would be more machinery than it saves, so we kept each small and independent. If the count grows, extracting a component will be the right move. Two small CSS lessons Row highlights need to reach the card’s true edge even when a scrollbar takes space, so the app measures the real scrollbar width once and feeds it into the layout as a CSS variable. And a table needs overflow-x: hidden set explicitly: leaving it unset lets it quietly compute to auto whenever the vertical overflow is set, which brings back a subtle horizontal scrollbar. The terminal screens on this site are real The terminal screenshots on our homepage are not drawn by hand. An ignored test fills otm with curated demo data, never your machine’s real processes or user names, renders its tabs into a test backend, and writes the result into the page. When the terminal UI changes, we re-run one command and the website follows. What we would do differently Filter thread entries in the core from day one ( we fixed it in 0.4.1 ). Make Services and Startup actions real earlier, instead of leaving them as interface-only. Persist App history to disk. Everything above is in the open on GitHub . If you would like to help with any of these, they are the best places to start. For why we chose this stack, see Tauri vs. Electron and Rust in the kernel .

title: Introducing Open Task Manager
desc: A free, open-source take on the Windows 11 Task Manager for Linux, Windows and macOS, plus a terminal UI called otm.
text: announcement Introducing Open Task Manager 2026-10-11 · sabaoongfx · 6 min read Almost everyone who uses a computer has opened a task manager at some point: the app froze, the fan started screaming, or the battery drained for no obvious reason. The Windows 11 Task Manager is a good answer to those moments. It groups processes by application, shows live graphs, and lets you end a stuck program in two clicks. The trouble is that it only exists on Windows, and you can’t read, change or audit it. Open Task Manager is our attempt to keep what works about that design and fix those two limits. It is a free, MIT-licensed process and performance monitor for Linux, Windows and macOS, with the layout you already know. This post covers what it is, how it is built, what it can and can’t do today, and where it is going. The idea Linux has plenty of system monitors, and many are excellent, but they each have their own conventions. macOS has Activity Monitor, which looks nothing like either. Anyone who switches between operating systems, or who supports family and coworkers on different ones, ends up re-learning the same tool three times. We wanted a single, familiar layout everywhere: a left-hand tab strip, a Processes list grouped by app, and a Performance page with CPU, memory, disk and network graphs. We also wanted it small, fast to start, and honest about what it does with your data. That last point gets its own post: Open Task Manager vs. the Windows Task Manager . What’s in the app Processes. Processes are grouped by application, so a browser with thirty helper processes appears as one expandable row. You can search, sort by any column, and end a task from the right-click menu or the keyboard. Performance. Live rolling charts for CPU, memory, disk and network, updated every 1.5 seconds from real operating-system counters. App history. Cumulative CPU time per application since the app was opened. Startup apps. The programs configured to launch at login. Users. Resource usage summed per user account, which is especially useful on shared machines and servers. Details. The flat, per-process table (PID, status, user, CPU, memory) for when you want the raw list instead of the grouped one. Services. The services configured on the machine. Disk usage. A WinDirStat-style scan of a folder showing what is using the space as a treemap, a tree, a largest-files list or a breakdown by file type. How it’s built Open Task Manager is a Cargo workspace with three parts that share one backend. core/ ( otm-core ) holds all data collection. It uses the sysinfo crate to read processes and hardware counters straight from the operating system, and keeps the rate and history state the graphs need. src-tauri/ is the desktop app. It is a thin layer of Tauri commands over the core, with a React and TypeScript interface drawn in your system’s own webview. tui/ is otm , the terminal version, built with ratatui. It calls the same core functions directly. Because the app uses the system webview instead of shipping its own copy of Chromium, installers stay small and memory use stays modest. A tool whose whole job is to show you what is eating your RAM shouldn’t be one of the biggest items on the list. Release builds also enable link-time optimization and symbol stripping, which keeps the binary compact. A terminal version: otm The same eight tabs are available without a desktop at all. otm is a keyboard- and mouse-driven terminal UI meant for SSH sessions, servers, and anyone who lives in a terminal. It reads the same real data through the same backend, and it needs no Node.js and no graphical session: cargo run -p otm On Linux, every package we publish installs both programs: the desktop app in your menu and otm on your path. Installing it We publish signed apt and pacman repositories, so on Ubuntu, Debian, Mint, Pop!_OS and Arch the app updates through your normal package manager. There are also .deb , .rpm and AppImage downloads, a Windows installer ( .exe and .msi ), and macOS disk images for Apple Silicon and Intel. Every direct download is listed in the download section , and standalone otm archives are attached to each release. What it can’t do yet We’d rather you hear the limits from us than discover them in the app, so here is the honest list. Ending a task is the only action that changes your system. Start/Stop on services and Enable/Disable on startup apps update the interface but don’t touch the real service manager or autostart entries yet. The Services and Startup tabs read real data on Linux only. On Windows and macOS they are currently empty in the installed app. App history resets when you close the app, because nothing is saved to disk. Windows and macOS installers are not code-signed yet, so you may see a warning the first time you open them. The roadmap tracks each of these, and the first two are the next priorities. Get involved The whole project is on GitHub . If you hit a bug, open an issue with your operating system and what you expected to see. If you want to help, the most valuable contributions right now are real service and startup control, testing on Windows and macOS, and the thread-counting fix. Since the code is open, you can also read exactly what the app does before you trust it with your machine.

title: Running AI Models Locally: How to Estimate the RAM You'll Need
desc: A simple formula for the memory a local language model needs, why quantization matters, and how to watch it in a task manager.
text: Trends Running AI Models Locally: How to Estimate the RAM You'll Need 2026-10-11 · sabaoongfx · 3 min read Running a language model on your own computer has become popular for privacy, cost and offline use. The first practical question is always the same: will it fit in memory? The honest answer is that you can estimate it with some arithmetic, then confirm it with a task manager. Be wary of web pages that give specific hardware tables without showing their working; many of those we found while researching this were generic or unreliable. The rule of thumb A model’s weights are a long list of numbers, and each number takes a fixed amount of space. So: weights memory (GB) ~= parameters (billions) x bits per weight / 8 A model with 7 billion parameters stored at 16 bits per weight needs about 14 GB. The same model compressed to 8 bits needs about 7 GB, and at 4 bits about 3.5 GB. That compression is called quantization : it trades a small loss in quality for a large saving in memory. What gets added on top The context cache. While generating, the model stores intermediate values (the key-value cache) for every token in the conversation. It grows with context length, and for long contexts it can reach gigabytes. Runtime overhead. The inference program itself, buffers and the operating system need room too. Everything else you have open. Your browser does not shrink because a model is loaded. A reasonable planning approach is to take the weights figure and add 20 to 30 percent for the cache and overhead, more if you use very long contexts. Treat it as a rough estimate; actual numbers depend on the model architecture and the software. Where the memory has to be Speed depends on where the weights live. On a computer with a dedicated graphics card, the weights ideally fit in the card’s own memory (VRAM), which is fast but limited. On machines with unified memory, such as many recent laptops, the processor and graphics share one pool, so total RAM is the limit. Models that don’t fit can spill into ordinary RAM or even onto disk, which works but can be many times slower. This is why memory prices matter for this use case in particular ( the 2026 crunch ): the capacity you need is set by the model, and it is the part of the machine you can’t easily trade away. Check it in a task manager Close what you can and note your baseline memory on the Performance tab. Load the model and watch the memory chart. The difference is its real footprint. Start a long conversation and watch it grow. That slope is the cache. If memory approaches the limit and disk activity jumps, the system is swapping and generation will crawl ( diagnosing a busy disk ). Check the CPU view. On machines without a suitable graphics card, inference uses the processor heavily, so expect sustained high load on many cores. Remember that one program may appear as several processes, so look at the grouped total. And since resident memory counts shared pages, a memory-mapped model file may show differently in different tools ( why ). Practical choices If memory is tight, choose a smaller model or a more aggressive quantization before buying hardware. Shorten the context you actually need. Close memory-hungry programs such as browsers while the model runs. The core idea is simple: the model’s size is a number you can compute, and the task manager is how you verify it. Do both before you spend money.

title: Memory Explained: RSS, Working Set, Shared and Cached
desc: Why the numbers in different monitors never match, why 'free' memory is not a goal, and how to read a memory column without panicking.
text: Fundamentals Memory Explained: RSS, Working Set, Shared and Cached 2026-10-11 · sabaoongfx · 3 min read Few numbers cause more confusion than memory. You close everything, and the monitor says half your RAM is used. Two tools disagree by a gigabyte. A program seems to use more than it could. None of this means something is broken: it means “memory used” is several different things with the same name. Virtual versus physical Every process sees a large, private range of virtual memory, an address space the operating system maps onto real RAM only as needed. A program can reserve gigabytes of address space and touch very little of it. Monitors that show virtual size look alarming and mean little. What matters day to day is how much physical RAM a process is actually holding. The common measures Resident set size (RSS) on Linux and macOS. The amount of a process’s memory currently in RAM. It includes pages shared with other processes, such as libraries, so adding RSS across processes counts shared pages repeatedly. Working set on Windows. The set of pages recently used and kept in RAM. It plays the same role as RSS and has a similar double-counting caveat. A related figure, private working set, excludes shared pages. Shared memory. Pages used by more than one process. The same library loaded by thirty programs can sit in RAM once. Private or unique memory. What would be freed if the process ended. It is the fairest measure of an app’s own cost, and harder to compute. The monitor you use picks one of these. Open Task Manager shows per-process memory as reported by the operating system through sysinfo , a resident-memory style number, so summing many processes can overstate the true total. This is the same effect that makes thread listings inflate memory . Why “used” is high on a healthy machine Unused RAM is wasted RAM, so operating systems fill spare memory with cache : recently read files and data kept in memory so the next access is fast. Cache is released instantly when programs need the space. On Linux, the “free” command separates it out; on Windows, Task Manager shows it as “cached” or “standby.” A machine showing 90 percent used with most of it cache is working as designed. That is why “RAM cleaner” tools are usually counterproductive. They discard the cache, so files you will need again must reload from disk, making the machine feel slower while the number looks better. Signs of real memory pressure The memory chart is pinned near the top and disk activity is high and constant, because the system is paging data to disk. The machine stutters when switching between apps that were fine a moment ago. Programs are closed or killed by the system. On Linux this is the out-of-memory killer, and its messages appear in the system log. A single process’s memory grows steadily and never falls ( a leak ). Reading a memory column well Look at the group total for an app, not one helper process. Watch the trend over minutes, not one instant. Compare against available memory, not total, since cache can be reclaimed. When two tools disagree, check which measure each uses before assuming one is wrong. With that in mind, memory prices matter more than they did last year ( here is why ), and reading the numbers correctly is the first step to spending less of it.

title: The MIT License, Explained for People Who Just Want to Use the Software
desc: What the license lets you do, what it asks of you, what it doesn't promise, and why it matters if you ever want to fork a tool.
text: Fundamentals The MIT License, Explained for People Who Just Want to Use the Software 2026-10-11 · sabaoongfx · 3 min read Open Task Manager is released under the MIT license, one of the most widely used open source licenses. Most people never read the license of the software they install. Here is what this one means in practice, in plain language. This is general information, not legal advice; read the license text itself, which is short, and talk to a lawyer if it matters for your business. What you are allowed to do The MIT license grants anyone who has a copy of the software permission, free of charge, to: Use it for any purpose, personal or commercial. Copy and modify it to suit your needs. Distribute it , in original or modified form. Sell it , or include it in something you sell. Combine it with other software, including proprietary software. That last point is why businesses like MIT-licensed code: it asks for very little back. What it asks of you There is one condition. If you distribute the software or substantial parts of it, you must include the original copyright notice and the license text. That is how credit is preserved. Nothing requires you to publish your own changes, to use the same license for your modifications or to notify the author. Licenses that do require sharing changes are usually called “copyleft” (the GPL is the best known); MIT is “permissive.” What it doesn’t promise The software is provided “as is,” without warranty of any kind, and the authors are not liable for damages. That is standard, and it is a fair description of how volunteer-maintained software works. It doesn’t mean the software is unreliable; it means nobody has promised you anything. For a tool that can end processes on your computer, it is sensible to be aware of that. Why it matters for a system monitor You can inspect it. The license gives you the right to read, build and run the code. Combined with the absence of telemetry code, you can confirm for yourself how it behaves. You can fork it. If development stops or goes in a direction you dislike, you or anyone else can continue it. This protects users from abandonment. You can package it. Linux distributions can include it, and companies can bundle it internally, with attribution. Note that a license covers the project’s own code. The libraries it uses have their own licenses, which are usually compatible with MIT but listed separately. If you redistribute, check them. What the license is not Not a privacy policy. A license describes your rights to the software, not what the software does with data. We cover that separately ( and show you how to check it ). Not a trademark grant. The right to use the code doesn’t automatically include the right to use the project’s name and logo in a way that implies endorsement. If you publish a fork, it’s courteous, and sometimes necessary, to rename it. Not a guarantee of safety. Open source code can still contain bugs ( and attackers target open source ), though it can be audited by anyone. If you want to contribute Contributing under MIT is simple: your changes are submitted under the same license as the project. Details are in the repository on GitHub . If you only want to use the app, none of this changes anything: install it and go.

title: Open Task Manager vs. the Windows Task Manager
desc: A fair comparison of Open Task Manager and the Windows Task Manager, and what open source does and does not mean for your privacy.
text: comparison & privacy Open Task Manager vs. the Windows Task Manager 2026-10-11 · sabaoongfx · 8 min read Open Task Manager copies the layout of the Windows 11 Task Manager on purpose. That makes the obvious question: if it looks the same, why use it? The honest answer is that for many Windows users, the built-in one is fine. This post lays out where the two differ, where the built-in one is still ahead, and what “open source” actually means for your privacy, without overstating it. The short version If you only use Windows and want the deepest integration, the built-in Task Manager is hard to beat. If you use Linux or macOS, or several systems, Open Task Manager gives you one familiar layout everywhere, and a terminal version too. If you care about being able to check what a tool does, Open Task Manager lets you. The Windows one is closed source, so you can’t. Side by side Windows Task Manager Open Task Manager Platforms Windows only Linux, Windows, macOS Source code Closed, not auditable Open, MIT license Terminal version No (separate tools such as tasklist ) Yes, otm with the same tabs Processes grouped by app Yes Yes Live CPU, memory, disk, network graphs Yes Yes Services and startup control Fully working Reads real data on Linux; start/stop and enable/disable are UI-only for now Depth of Windows-specific data Extensive, built into the OS Cross-platform subset Network use by the app itself Not documented as sending data; can’t be verified None in the code; you can check Install Ships with Windows apt, pacman, .deb, .rpm, AppImage, .exe/.msi, .dmg Price Included with Windows Free Where the Windows one is still better A fair comparison has to start here. The built-in Task Manager is part of the operating system, and it uses Windows-only interfaces that a portable tool can’t reach with the same depth. It controls services and startup items for real, and it surfaces Windows-specific details that a cross-platform app doesn’t attempt to match. It also needs no installation, no download and no trust decision, because it is already there. Open Task Manager is also younger. As of version 0.4.2, Windows and macOS installers are unsigned, app history isn’t saved between sessions, and the Services and Startup controls don’t yet change the system. We list these on the roadmap because pretending otherwise would waste your time. Where Open Task Manager is different It runs where Windows doesn’t. On Linux and macOS the alternatives are different tools with different layouts. Here you get the same Processes, Performance, App history, Startup apps, Users, Details and Services tabs on all three. It has a terminal mode. otm shows the same eight tabs over SSH on a headless server, with no desktop session and no Node.js. Windows has no built-in equivalent with the same layout. It is small and native. It is built on Tauri and Rust and uses your system’s webview rather than bundling a browser engine, so the installer is small and the monitor itself doesn’t become the heaviest thing running. You can change it. Want another column, a different refresh rate or a bug fixed? The code is there. You can fork it, patch it and run your version. The privacy question, answered carefully The claim in the title of this section is easy to exaggerate in both directions, so here is exactly what we can and can’t say. What we can say about Open Task Manager Open Task Manager has no telemetry and no background service . This isn’t just a promise. You can verify it yourself: The Rust code declares only a few direct dependencies: sysinfo for reading the machine, serde for formatting data, Tauri for the window, and ratatui for the terminal UI. None of the three crates in the workspace lists an HTTP client, analytics library or crash-reporting service. In the app’s source, the only web address in the configuration is localhost:1420 , the development server used when building the app. Nothing points to a remote server. Process data is read from your operating system, shown in the window, and discarded. App history lives in memory only, which is why it resets when you close the app. The program runs only while its window is open. There is no helper process or scheduled task left behind. If you don’t want to take our word for it, build it from source, or watch its network activity with a firewall or a tool such as Wireshark. A tool with nothing to hide gives you nothing to find. What we can’t say about the Windows Task Manager We have no evidence that the Windows Task Manager itself sends your process list anywhere, and we aren’t claiming it does. What we can say is more modest and still important: Windows as a whole does collect diagnostic data, Microsoft documents settings that control how much, and the Task Manager is closed source, so an outside observer can’t read what it does. You are trusting the vendor’s description rather than checking the code. That is the real difference. “Open source” doesn’t automatically mean “private”. A project can be open and still be careless with your data. What it gives you is verifiability : anyone, including security researchers who don’t know us, can read the code, build it, and confirm that it does what we say. If we ever added tracking, it would be visible in the repository history for everyone to see. Limits of this claim Open Task Manager runs on top of an operating system. If that system collects data, this app doesn’t change it. Installing from the apt, pacman or GitHub download servers means those hosts see your download request, as with any software. The website you are reading is a separate static site. The live demo embedded on it runs on generated sample data, not on your machine’s processes. Which should you use? On a single Windows PC, keep using the built-in one for services and startup management, and try Open Task Manager if you want to compare. On Linux or macOS, or across several machines, or on servers you reach over SSH, Open Task Manager gives you one consistent tool. And if auditability matters to you, it is the one whose behaviour you can check yourself. You can try the interface right now in the live demo , or grab an installer from the download section . The source is on GitHub . If you find a claim in this post that the code doesn’t support, please open an issue and we’ll correct it.

title: Process vs. Thread: Why Some Linux Monitors Show Thousands of Entries
desc: Threads share a process's memory, but some Linux tools list each as its own row. Here is the difference, and why it can inflate counts and memory totals.
text: Fundamentals Process vs. Thread: Why Some Linux Monitors Show Thousands of Entries 2026-10-11 · sabaoongfx · 3 min read If you have used a monitor on Linux and wondered why it listed thousands of entries and more memory than your machine has, you may have met the process-versus-thread problem. It is a good example of how the same data can be read two ways. We hit it ourselves: versions of Open Task Manager before 0.4.1 showed exactly this on Linux. Two ways to do more than one thing A process is an isolated running program with its own private memory. A thread is a path of execution inside a process. Threads of the same process share its memory, which makes them cheap to create and lets them cooperate easily, but also means a bug in one can affect the others. A single-threaded program can only do one thing at a time. A multi-threaded program can, for example, keep its interface responsive while downloading a file on another thread. Modern apps routinely have dozens of threads, and a browser or game may have hundreds. How Linux represents them Linux treats both as “tasks” internally. Each thread gets its own ID in the kernel, and the first thread of a process is the one whose ID is shown as the process’s PID. In the /proc filesystem, threads appear in a per-process folder. Some libraries that list processes on Linux walk that data in a way that surfaces each thread as an entry of its own. Open Task Manager reads its data through the sysinfo crate, and on Linux that library can list every thread as a separate process. Before version 0.4.1 we passed all of them through. The catch is what each entry reports: because threads share memory, each one reports the memory of the whole process. Add them up and you count the same memory many times. What goes wrong Inflated process counts. A machine with 300 real processes can show over a thousand rows. Impossible memory totals. Summing per-row memory, as a Users view does, can exceed the physical RAM installed. Misleading sorting. A process with many threads can appear many times near the top. The fix was straightforward: skip entries that the library identifies as threads when building the snapshot, which version 0.4.1 does. Process counts and memory totals dropped as a result and now line up with what the machine really has. It is worth knowing about because other tools still make the same mistake. How to tell if a tool is doing this Compare the monitor’s total against the machine. Add the memory of the largest groups and see whether it plausibly fits in your RAM. Compare the process count with the output of a basic command such as ps -e | wc -l , which counts processes rather than threads. Large mismatches suggest threads are being listed. Some tools offer a toggle to show or hide threads, and htop , for example, can show them as a tree you can switch off. Why you might want threads anyway Showing threads is not wrong; it answers a different question. If you are debugging why one program is slow, a per-thread view can show that a single thread is pegging a core while the others idle. That is invaluable for developers. For everyday use, though, a process-level view with accurate totals is what people expect from a task manager. For the related question of what a percentage of CPU means across threads and cores, see CPU usage explained . If you are new to the vocabulary, start with what a process is .

title: The 2026 RAM Price Crunch: Why Knowing Where Your Memory Goes Matters
desc: Memory prices have jumped sharply this year as AI data centers absorb supply. Here is what is happening, and why wasting RAM is more expensive than it used to be.
text: Trends The 2026 RAM Price Crunch: Why Knowing Where Your Memory Goes Matters 2026-10-11 · sabaoongfx · 3 min read If you shopped for a laptop or a memory upgrade this year, you probably noticed the prices. DRAM and flash storage have become markedly more expensive in 2026, and the reason is not a mystery: the companies that make memory chips are selling more of their output to AI data centers, which pay more and buy in bulk. Consumers are getting what is left. What the reports say Estimates vary by source and by which chip type they measure, so treat the specifics as ranges: One analysis reported LPDDR5X prices up 89 percent and DDR4 up to 51 percent in the second quarter of 2026. Another put the first-quarter jump at roughly 95 percent. TrendForce estimated that AI-focused systems would consume about 70 percent of global memory hardware production this year. Micron shut down its Crucial consumer memory business, removing a well-known brand from shelves. Laptops from Dell, HP and Lenovo reportedly rose 15 to 30 percent, and Gartner estimated that combined DRAM and SSD prices would rise about 130 percent by the end of 2026 compared with 2025. On timing, Gartner has said shortages could extend into the second half of 2027, IDC said “well into 2027,” and one outlet suggested normalisation may not come before 2028. Forecasts like these are often wrong in both directions, so the safe reading is simple: memory is expensive now and is likely to stay that way for a while. Why this changes how you should think about RAM For most of the last decade you could fix a slow machine by adding memory cheaply. When memory costs more, the cheaper fix becomes using what you have more carefully. And the other side of the market has made the problem worse: a configuration with less RAM at the same sticker price is now a common way for prices to “hold.” Check the spec, not just the model name. It also changes which software is worth keeping. A handful of applications account for most of your memory use, and they are often not the ones you would guess. That is the use case for a task manager’s Processes view sorted by memory: a two-minute look often shows a browser with a hundred tabs, a chat app that never quits, or a background updater, and closing one can free more than a hardware upgrade would. A five-minute memory audit Open the Processes tab and sort by Memory , with processes grouped by application so helpers add up under one row. Write down the top five. Ask of each: do I need this running right now? Check the Performance tab’s memory chart. A flat line well below the maximum means you probably don’t need more RAM. A line pinned at the top with heavy disk activity means you do, or that something is leaking (see how to find a memory leak ). Open Startup apps and disable anything that doesn’t need to launch at login. We cover the habits in more depth in our practical guide to stretching your RAM . Buying advice, briefly If you are choosing hardware, compare RAM and storage between models explicitly, because specs may have been trimmed to hold a price. If you can upgrade later, buy the machine with the slots and upgrade when prices fall. If you can’t, buy the larger configuration once rather than planning to add memory afterwards. Either way, measure before you spend: a free monitor can tell you whether memory was ever your bottleneck.

title: Reading the Network Graph: Which App Is Using Your Bandwidth?
desc: How to read throughput numbers, find the application behind a spike, and tell normal background traffic from something worth investigating.
text: How-to Reading the Network Graph: Which App Is Using Your Bandwidth? 2026-10-11 · sabaoongfx · 2 min read A slow video call, a download that stalls, a data cap that vanishes: all of these start with the question “what is using my network?” A task manager can answer part of it quickly. This guide explains what the numbers mean, what they can't tell you, and where to go for the rest. What the graph shows The network section of the Performance view plots the data your machine is receiving and sending, summed across all of its network interfaces: Wi-Fi, Ethernet, virtual adapters. In Open Task Manager, the rates come from the operating system’s interface counters and are reported as bytes per second, refreshed every 1.5 seconds. You will usually see two lines: receive (download) and transmit (upload). A few reading tips: Bytes versus bits. Internet plans are advertised in bits per second; monitors often show bytes. Multiply by eight to compare. 10 MB/s is about 80 Mbit/s. Download and upload are separate. A cloud backup shows as sustained upload. A video stream shows as sustained download. Virtual interfaces count. VPNs, containers and virtual machines add interfaces, and traffic can be counted on more than one. If numbers look doubled, check the interface list. Finding the application The machine-wide graph tells you that something is using the network. Finding what is more variable. Some operating systems report network use per process; others, and some monitors, show only the totals. Windows Task Manager and Resource Monitor include a per-process network column. On Linux, per-process bandwidth generally needs a dedicated tool such as nethogs , which watches traffic by process. We don’t claim Open Task Manager attributes network use to individual processes; it shows interface totals, so use it to confirm a spike and another tool to name the culprit. A practical routine: Watch the graph while you close apps one at a time. When the line drops, you found the source. Pause cloud sync, backups and updates first; they are the usual offenders. Check your browser: video, a stuck page, or a background tab can stream continuously. If the traffic continues with everything closed, a different device on your network may be responsible, so check your router’s client list. Normal versus suspicious Small, regular bursts are normal: time sync, update checks, notifications. What deserves a closer look is large, sustained upload from something that shouldn’t have a reason to send data, or steady traffic at night from an app you never use. Those patterns are worth investigating with the methods in how to check what an app sends over the network . Limits of a task manager here A throughput graph shows volume, not content or destination. It can’t tell you whether traffic is encrypted, where it is going, or whether it is wanted. Treat it as a smoke detector: it says there is something worth looking at, and the other tools say what. That is also why we make no claim about network contents on this site beyond what our code does, which is open for you to read.

title: How to Reduce Windows Diagnostic Data Collection: The Settings That Matter
desc: A short, honest walkthrough of the Windows privacy settings that control diagnostic data, what they do and don't change, and why to re-check them after updates.
text: Privacy How to Reduce Windows Diagnostic Data Collection: The Settings That Matter 2026-10-11 · sabaoongfx · 3 min read Windows collects diagnostic data about how the system and its apps behave, and Microsoft documents that collection and lets you control part of it. This guide covers the settings most people mean when they ask how to turn telemetry down, and is upfront about what these switches can and can’t do. We aren’t privacy lawyers, and we aren’t claiming that Windows is doing something sinister. The goal is to help you make informed choices. The two switches to start with Open Settings > Privacy & security > Diagnostics & feedback . Reporting from PCWorld recommends turning off two options here: Send optional diagnostic data. Windows separates data it describes as required from data it describes as optional. Turning the optional setting off limits what is sent to the required set. Tailored experiences. This uses your diagnostic data to personalise tips and suggestions. Turning it off stops that personalisation. Menu names and layout change between Windows versions, so if you don’t see exactly these labels, look for the same terms nearby and check Microsoft’s current documentation. Things worth reviewing next Activity history and advertising ID. Both sit in the Privacy & security section and are easy to switch off if you don’t use them. App permissions. The same section lists which apps can use your location, camera, microphone and files. Many people have never opened it. Optional features such as Recall. If your hardware offers them, read what they store before enabling. We discuss the reasoning in Windows Recall and the case for software you can audit . Account type. A local account sends less to a cloud account than a Microsoft account, though it also loses sync features. What these switches don’t do Be realistic about the limits. Turning off optional diagnostic data reduces what is sent but does not stop all communication: Windows still checks for updates, and required diagnostic data continues. Home and Pro editions generally can’t reduce collection below the required level through the Settings app. Third-party apps have their own data practices that these settings don’t touch. One more caution: some users report that updates re-enable settings they had switched off. That is a user report rather than something we have confirmed, but it is cheap to guard against. Re-open the page after major feature updates and confirm your choices held. See what is actually running Settings tell you what is permitted. A task manager tells you what is running. Open the Processes view and look through the list for background items you don’t recognise, then research a name before deciding anything. The Startup apps tab shows what launches with Windows. This won’t reveal network traffic on its own, and for that you need the approach in how to check what an app sends over the network . A sensible stance You don’t have to choose between ignoring privacy and abandoning your operating system. A reasonable middle path is to switch off the optional settings, review app permissions once a quarter, prefer software you can inspect for tools that watch your activity, and keep your system updated. Privacy is made of many small decisions, and none of them needs to be dramatic.

title: Rust Is Now a Permanent Part of the Linux Kernel. Here's What That Means for System Tools
desc: Kernel maintainers ended the Rust experiment in December 2025. What changed, what didn't, and why it matters for the tools that monitor your machine.
text: Trends Rust Is Now a Permanent Part of the Linux Kernel. Here's What That Means for System Tools 2026-10-11 · sabaoongfx · 3 min read In December 2025, at the Maintainers Summit in Tokyo, Linux kernel developers reached a consensus that Rust in the kernel is no longer an experiment. Miguel Ojeda, who leads the Rust for Linux effort, sent a patch removing the “experimental” warnings from the kernel documentation and summed it up in one line: “The experiment is over, meaning Rust stays.” For a project that began as a curiosity a few years earlier, that is a large shift in status. What actually changed It is worth being precise, because headlines made this sound bigger than it is. Nobody is rewriting the kernel in Rust. The C code that makes up almost all of Linux is staying. What changed is the policy: Rust is now a supported, permanent way to write new kernel code, mainly drivers and other self-contained subsystems, and the project will keep investing in the build tooling and the abstractions that make it work. Ojeda was also careful to say this does not mean everything works for every kernel configuration, processor architecture or toolchain. A lot of work remains, and some maintainers still have reservations about mixed-language code. Reports also note that Android 16 devices built on the 6.12 kernel already ship a memory allocator called ashmem written in Rust, so the language is running on a very large number of phones today. Why memory safety is the point Operating system code spends its life handling raw memory: buffers, pointers, lifetimes. In C, a single mistake such as reading past the end of a buffer or using memory after it has been freed can become a crash or a security hole. Rust’s compiler rules out entire categories of those mistakes before the program runs, without needing a garbage collector. That trade is the reason kernel developers were willing to take on the cost of supporting a second language. The same logic applies one level up. A system monitor reads untrusted, constantly changing data from the operating system: process names that can contain any bytes, files that vanish between listing and opening, counters that wrap. A tool in a memory-safe language can still have bugs, but a misread buffer is much less likely to become something worse. What it means for the tools you use For the ordinary person running Linux, nothing visible changes today. Over the next few years you may notice more drivers and utilities written in Rust, and fewer of the memory-corruption bugs that fill security advisories. For tool authors, the signal is that Rust is a safe long-term bet: if the most conservative large codebase in open source is committing to it, a smaller project can too. That is part of why Open Task Manager is built the way it is. Its data-collection library, otm-core , is written in Rust and shared by the desktop app and the terminal UI, so the code that touches your operating system is the code the compiler checks most strictly. The interface above it is TypeScript and React inside a native Tauri window. If you want a closer look at that split, how we built Open Task Manager walks through it. What to watch Driver coverage. The first real test is how many in-tree drivers adopt Rust, and how smoothly they are maintained. Toolchain stability. The kernel depends on specific compiler features, so how quickly those become stable matters for distributions. The human side. Mixed-language projects live or die on whether maintainers of different languages can work together. The summit outcome helps, but it is not the end of that conversation. The takeaway is modest and useful: Rust in the kernel is no longer a bet on the future, it is part of the present. That is good news for anyone who cares about the reliability of the software that sits closest to the hardware.

title: Rust Is the Most Admired Language Again. Does It Matter for Desktop Apps?
desc: The 2025 Stack Overflow survey put Rust on top for the tenth year running, but admiration and adoption are different things. What it means for desktop software.
text: Trends Rust Is the Most Admired Language Again. Does It Matter for Desktop Apps? 2026-10-11 · sabaoongfx · 3 min read The 2025 Stack Overflow Developer Survey, with more than 49,000 responses from 177 countries, again named Rust the most admired programming language, at 72 percent. Gleam followed at 70 percent, Elixir at 66 and Zig at 64. Cargo, Rust’s package manager, was the most admired cloud and infrastructure tool at 71 percent, and uv, a Python package manager written in Rust, scored 74 percent in the technologies category. Numbers like these invite two lazy reactions: “everything will be rewritten in Rust” and “it is just hype.” Neither is right, and the useful answer sits in between. What “admired” measures The survey asks developers who have used a language whether they want to keep using it. So “admired” is a satisfaction score among people who already tried it. It says nothing about how many people use the language, and it is skewed toward people who chose Rust on purpose. A language that is hard to start with can score well because the people who got past the learning curve are happy. That caveat matters, but the result has been consistent for years, and it lines up with other signals: Rust’s permanent place in the Linux kernel, the growing number of command-line tools written in it, and the wave of Python and JavaScript tooling that has moved to it for speed. The survey’s own Cargo and uv numbers fit the same pattern. Why desktop software cares Desktop programs have a different set of pressures from web services. They start often, they run alongside dozens of other programs, and users notice every extra megabyte. Rust gives three things that suit that environment: Predictable performance. There is no garbage collector pausing the program, so memory use and latency stay steady. Small, self-contained binaries. A release build can be a single executable with its dependencies compiled in. Safety at the edges. Code that talks to the operating system is exactly where memory bugs hurt most. The cost is real too. Rust has a steep learning curve, compile times can be long, and the graphical-interface ecosystem is younger than the options in C++, C# or JavaScript. That last point is why many Rust desktop apps pair a Rust core with a web-based interface, which is the approach we took. The tradeoffs of that choice are covered in Tauri vs. Electron: what the numbers say . A practical way to read the survey If you are choosing a language for a desktop tool, treat the survey as a tiebreaker, not a decision. Ask instead: Will the people maintaining this be comfortable in it in three years? Does the library you need exist? Can you hire or attract contributors? For a system monitor, the answers favoured Rust: the sysinfo crate already handles the per-platform differences in reading processes and hardware, and a single Rust core can feed both a graphical app and a terminal UI. The honest summary is that Rust’s popularity is real, well-measured among its users, and backed by serious adoption in places that are hard to fake, like the kernel. It is not a guarantee of a good product. A badly designed tool in any language is still a badly designed tool.

title: Services Explained: What Runs in the Background on Linux and Windows
desc: What a service is, how systemd and the Windows Services manager differ, and why you should look before you stop one.
text: Fundamentals Services Explained: What Runs in the Background on Linux and Windows 2026-10-11 · sabaoongfx · 3 min read Many programs on your computer don’t have a window. They start with the system, run in the background, and do jobs such as managing the network, printing, syncing the clock or serving a website. These are services (called daemons on Unix-like systems), and they are a large part of what the Services tab in a task manager shows. What makes a service different An ordinary program starts when a person launches it and ends when they close it. A service is managed by the operating system: it can start at boot with no one logged in, restart automatically if it crashes, and depend on other services starting first. That is what lets a server run unattended for months. Windows Windows lists services in the Services app and in Task Manager’s Services tab. Each has a name, description, status (running or stopped) and a startup type : automatic, automatic (delayed), manual or disabled. Many belong to Windows itself; others are installed by drivers and applications. They typically run under special accounts such as System or Local Service. Linux and systemd Most mainstream Linux distributions use systemd to manage services, which it calls units . A unit file describes what to run, when, and under what conditions. You inspect them with systemctl : systemctl status name shows the current state, and systemctl list-units --type=service lists them. States include active (running), inactive and failed. Open Task Manager’s Services tab reads its list from the output of systemctl on Linux. Distributions without systemd use other init systems, and this tab shows nothing there. Honest status of this tab Reading works on Linux, with real data. Start and Stop buttons update the interface only. They do not yet send commands to systemd. Windows and macOS do not populate the Services list in the installed app yet. For real control today, use systemctl on Linux or the Services app on Windows. The Windows tool is more complete at present, and we say so in our comparison . Before you stop a service Read its description. If you can’t tell what it does, search the name first. Check what depends on it. Stopping the network service takes the network with it, and stopping the display manager ends your session. Prefer restart over stop for a misbehaving service. Many problems clear with a restart. Prefer disabling over deleting. Disabled services can be re-enabled; deleted ones may not be recoverable. Write down what you changed. If something breaks tomorrow, you’ll want to undo it. Why look at services at all Services are where background resource use hides. A single runaway service can use a core, hold memory or hammer the disk, and it never shows up as a window you could close. If the Processes view shows a system-owned process at the top of CPU or disk and you can't explain it, the Services view often names the cause. It is also where servers reveal what they are running, which is why a terminal version matters when you manage a machine remotely ( see our comparison ).

title: How to Stretch Your RAM: A Practical Guide for Any Operating System
desc: Eight habits that reduce memory use on Windows, Linux and macOS, with how to check that each one actually helped.
text: How-to How to Stretch Your RAM: A Practical Guide for Any Operating System 2026-10-11 · sabaoongfx · 3 min read With memory prices up, the cheapest upgrade is the one you don’t buy. Most computers waste a surprising amount of RAM on things nobody asked for. This guide gives you eight habits that work on any operating system, and, importantly, a way to confirm each one actually helped, so you don’t spend an afternoon on a change that did nothing. First, take a baseline Restart the machine, open nothing, and wait two minutes. Open a task manager and write down total memory in use from the Performance tab. This is your floor.
