Everything above it is something you opened or something that started on its own. Without this number, you can’t tell later whether you improved anything. The eight habits Sort by memory and read the top five. Use the grouped Processes view so an app and its helpers show as one row. Most people find one or two surprises. Trim startup apps. Chat clients, updaters, cloud-sync tools and launchers often start with the system and stay resident. Disable the ones you open only occasionally. Our startup guide has a decision rule. Tame the browser. Browsers use a separate process per tab or site, and each costs memory. Close tabs you aren’t using, use the browser’s built-in tab-sleeping option if it has one, and watch which extensions are large. See why browsers use so much memory . Quit, don’t just close. On macOS and Linux, closing a window often leaves the program running. On Windows, many apps sit in the system tray. A task manager shows what is still alive. Prefer lighter alternatives for always-on tools. A chat app that bundles its own browser engine can use hundreds of megabytes while idle. A native or web-view-based alternative may use far less. Measure, don’t assume. Restart long-running apps. Some programs slowly grow over days. Restarting the worst one weekly costs nothing. Watch for leaks. If one process only ever grows, that is a bug, not a feature. Here is how to confirm it . Only then consider hardware. If the memory chart is pinned and disk activity is high even after the above, you are genuinely short of RAM. What not to do Don’t use “RAM cleaner” utilities. They mostly force the system to drop its cache, which makes everything reload from disk and feel slower. See memory explained for why free memory is not a goal. Don’t end processes you can’t identify. Search the name first. Ending a system process can log you out or freeze the desktop. Don’t judge by one reading. Memory moves. Watch a minute of the chart, not a single instant. Check that it worked After your changes, restart, wait the same two minutes, and read the same number. If your idle baseline dropped, the startup changes helped. Then open your usual set of apps and compare again. A drop of a few hundred megabytes is normal; a drop of a gigabyte means you found something big. All of this works with the tool that ships with your OS. We suggest Open Task Manager mainly because it gives you the same view on every system, which helps if you use more than one computer.

title: Shai-Hulud and the Case for Small Dependency Trees
desc: The 2025 npm worm showed how one compromised package can spread. What happened, what it means for any app you install, and the habits that reduce your exposure.
text: Security Shai-Hulud and the Case for Small Dependency Trees 2026-10-11 · sabaoongfx · 3 min read In September 2025, attackers compromised the accounts of maintainers of popular npm packages, including well-known utilities such as debug and chalk , and published tainted versions. A related campaign, nicknamed Shai-Hulud after the sandworms of Dune , went further: its install script stole developer credentials and used them to republish infected versions of the victims’ own packages, reportedly reaching more than 180 packages. Security firms described it as among the first self-replicating supply chain attacks. In November 2025 a second wave, usually called Shai-Hulud 2.0, moved the malicious code to the preinstall stage, widened its reach to Linux, macOS and Windows, and added further spreading mechanisms. Packages uploaded between November 21 and 23 reportedly affected projects from companies including Zapier, PostHog and Postman. Counts and details vary between security vendors, so treat exact numbers as approximate. Why this matters even if you never use npm Most modern software is assembled from hundreds of third-party packages, in every language. When you install an app, you inherit trust in every one of them. A compromised package doesn’t have to be famous; it only has to be somewhere in the chain. And for a developer, the first thing a malicious install script reaches is the credentials on the machine that is building the software you will later download. Where a system monitor stands A system monitor is a sensitive kind of program: it reads every process on your machine. That is a strong argument for it to have few moving parts. In Open Task Manager’s case, the Rust workspace declares only a few direct dependencies: sysinfo , serde , Tauri and ratatui. The web interface lists six runtime packages (React, ReactDOM, the Tauri API and opener plugin, an Inter font package and an icon set), with the build tools kept separate as development dependencies. Lockfiles for both ecosystems are committed to the repository. We should be careful about what that does and doesn’t prove. Every direct dependency brings its own dependencies, and the full tree is much larger than six or four. A short list is easier to review and gives an attacker fewer doors, but it is not immunity. Habits that reduce your exposure If you build software Commit and use lockfiles so installs are repeatable, and review dependency updates instead of accepting them automatically. Prefer fewer, well-maintained dependencies. Before adding a package for one small function, consider writing the function. Avoid running install scripts you don’t need. Package managers let you disable lifecycle scripts, which blocks the mechanism these worms used. Protect maintainer accounts with hardware-backed two-factor authentication and short-lived tokens. If you only install apps Prefer software from signed repositories or official releases over random download sites. Keep the system updated, since many incidents are caught and fixed quickly. Notice what new software does after install. A tool that has no reason to use the network but does is worth investigating ( here is how ). The bigger point Open source is not a defence against supply chain attacks; the affected packages were open source. What it does provide is visibility, because the malicious versions were found and analysed by outsiders reading public code and registries. Combine that visibility with small dependency trees and careful installs, and you reduce the odds that you are the one who finds out the hard way. We say more about why signed repositories matter in why signed package repositories matter .

title: Tauri vs. Electron: What the Numbers Say, and What They Don't
desc: Everyone quotes 3 MB versus 100 MB. Here is the range of figures published in 2026, why they disagree, and how to measure your own app.
text: Trends Tauri vs. Electron: What the Numbers Say, and What They Don't 2026-10-11 · sabaoongfx · 3 min read Almost every comparison of Tauri and Electron opens with a table showing Tauri winning by a wide margin. The direction is right. The exact numbers are much less reliable than they look, and it is worth knowing why before you quote them. The basic difference Electron bundles a full copy of Chromium and Node.js with every app. That gives you an identical rendering engine on every operating system, but each app carries its own browser. Tauri takes the opposite approach: the app uses the web view that already ships with the operating system (WebView2 on Windows, WebKit on macOS and Linux), and the backend is written in Rust. Less is bundled, so there is less to download and, usually, less to keep in memory. What published comparisons report A survey of 2026 articles shows a consistent direction and inconsistent figures: Installed size. One source reports a hello-world Tauri build near 3 MB against about 96 MB for Electron on Windows. Another gives Tauri apps 2 to 10 MB against 80 to 200 MB for Electron. Idle memory. One comparison puts a single window at around 80 MB for Tauri versus around 160 MB for Electron. Another claims 30 to 50 MB for Tauri. A third says Tauri uses roughly half as much, without naming its benchmark. Startup time. One report gives 380 ms for Tauri against 1,420 ms for Electron; another gives about 190 ms against about 640 ms on an M2 MacBook Air. Those memory figures differ by a factor of two or more from each other. That is not a contradiction so much as a sign that these are different apps, different operating systems, different Electron versions (the articles cite everything from 33 to 40) and different ways of counting memory. Some of the sources are also vendor-adjacent blogs rather than independent benchmarks. Why memory is hard to compare Electron runs several processes: a main process, one or more renderers, and helpers. Tauri’s web view is also multi-process on some platforms, and part of its memory is owned by the operating system, not by your app. So “how much does it use” depends on whether you count shared pages, whether you add up every child process, and which tool you used. We explain the counting problem in memory explained . The fair method is to sum all of an app’s processes in a single tool and compare like with like. What the numbers leave out Tauri’s advantages come with real costs: Rendering differences. Because each platform uses a different web view, a layout or feature can behave differently on Windows, macOS and Linux. Electron gives you one engine everywhere. Ecosystem maturity. Electron has years more tooling, documentation and answered questions. A second language. Backend work means Rust. That is a strength for performance and safety and a barrier for teams that only know JavaScript. Measure it yourself If the choice matters for your project, build the same small screen both ways and compare. Launch each, wait thirty seconds for it to settle, then open a task manager, group by application and read the combined memory of every process belonging to the app. Do it on each operating system you support. Open Task Manager’s Processes tab groups child processes under one row for exactly this kind of check. We chose Tauri for this project because a tool that reports what is using your memory should not itself be a heavy item on the list. We haven’t published a head-to-head benchmark of our own, and we would rather say so than borrow someone else’s numbers.

title: top, htop, btop and otm: Choosing a Terminal System Monitor
desc: A fair comparison of the terminal monitors people actually use, when each one is the right pick, and where the newcomer falls short.
text: Linux top, htop, btop and otm: Choosing a Terminal System Monitor 2026-10-11 · sabaoongfx · 3 min read If you manage a server over SSH, run a machine with no desktop, or just prefer a keyboard, a terminal system monitor is the tool you will reach for most. There are several good ones, and the right choice depends on what you value. Here is how the common options compare, including our own, which is the youngest and should not be assumed to be the best. top top ships with essentially every Unix-like system. That is its whole advantage: on a minimal server, a rescue shell or an unfamiliar machine, it is already there. It shows processes sorted by CPU, summary lines for load and memory, and a handful of interactive keys. The interface is austere and the learning curve for its commands is steeper than newer tools, but you can count on it. htop htop is the long-time favourite upgrade. It adds colour, per-core bars, a scrollable process list, a tree view that shows parent and child relationships, mouse support and easy kill and nice commands. It is mature, widely packaged and fast. If you want one tool to learn on Linux, this is the safe pick. btop btop leans into visuals: graphs for CPU, memory, disk and network on one dashboard, themes, and mouse control. It reads like a small control room. It tends to use more screen space and may need a modern terminal with Unicode support to look right. Its strength is giving a quick overall picture of the machine. Glances Glances, written in Python, collects a wide range of metrics and can run in a web or client-server mode, which is handy for watching remote systems. It is broader than a simple process viewer, at the cost of being heavier than the C and C++ tools above. otm otm is Open Task Manager’s terminal UI. Its angle is consistency: it presents the same eight tabs as the desktop app (Processes, Performance, App history, Startup apps, Users, Details, Services and Disk usage), reading from the same Rust data core. It supports keyboard and mouse input and groups processes by application. If you already use the graphical app or the Windows 11 Task Manager, the layout will be familiar. Install it with the desktop app on Linux, or download the standalone archive for your platform from the releases page. It is also the least proven. It does not yet have htop ’s years of polish, plugin-like flexibility or tree-style process view, and it shares the app’s known limits: its Services and Startup controls do not yet change the system, and App history resets when it closes. (Older versions also listed Linux threads as separate processes, explained here .) Which should you pick? You want Try Something that is already installed everywhere top The best all-round interactive tool htop A dashboard with graphs btop Remote or web monitoring, many metrics Glances The same layout as a desktop task manager otm A few habits that apply to all of them Learn how to sort by memory and by CPU, and how to filter by name. Know the difference between asking a process to quit and killing it ( here ). Read the load and memory summary before blaming one process. Don’t run monitors you haven’t verified as root on production systems without reading what they do. There is no need to pick only one. Many administrators keep top as a fallback, htop as a daily driver and something else for dashboards. Try each for a week and keep the one that stays out of your way.

title: What Is a Process? A Beginner's Guide to Reading Your Task Manager
desc: Every program you run becomes one or more processes. Learn what they are, what the columns mean, and which ones are safe to ignore.
text: Fundamentals What Is a Process? A Beginner's Guide to Reading Your Task Manager 2026-10-11 · sabaoongfx · 3 min read Open any task manager and you will see a long list of names, most of which you didn’t start on purpose. That list is made of processes , and understanding them turns the screen from noise into information. This guide assumes no background. A process is a running program A program is a file on disk: instructions waiting to be used. A process is what you get when the operating system loads those instructions into memory and starts running them. Open the same program twice and you may get two processes from one file. Each process gets its own private slice of memory, a unique number called a process ID (PID), and an owner, meaning the user account it runs as. The operating system keeps processes apart on purpose. One crashing program shouldn’t take down the others, and one program shouldn’t be able to read another’s memory. That separation is why you can end a frozen app without restarting the computer. Why one app is many processes Modern applications often split themselves across many processes. A web browser typically runs a main process, a separate process for each site or tab, a GPU process and several helpers. This improves stability and security, and it is also why the list looks so long. A good task manager groups these under the application so you can read the total at a glance. Open Task Manager’s Processes tab does this, and the Details tab shows the flat list when you need individual PIDs. The columns, in plain words Name. The program or app. Technical names can be cryptic; search the web before ending one you don’t recognise. PID. The unique number identifying that process while it runs. It is reused later, so don’t treat it as permanent. CPU. How much processor time it is using. What the percentage means depends on the tool. Memory. How much RAM it holds. This one is subtle; see memory explained . Disk and network. How much data it is reading, writing or sending right now. User. The account it runs as. Processes owned by “root” or “SYSTEM” belong to the operating system itself. Which processes are normal Most of the list is the operating system and your desktop doing housekeeping: window management, audio, networking, indexing, update checks. A fresh machine at rest might show a hundred or more entries. That is not a sign of trouble. Look instead for these patterns: One process using a lot of CPU for a long time when you aren’t doing anything. A process whose memory only goes up ( a possible leak ). An unfamiliar name running from an unusual place or as an unexpected user. What you can safely do You can end any application you started yourself. If it is frozen, ending its process is the standard fix, and the steps are in how to end a stuck process safely . You should leave alone anything owned by the system that you can’t identify; ending the wrong one can log you out or freeze the desktop. When in doubt, note the name, search it, and come back. A first exercise Open your task manager, sort by memory, and expand the top entry. Count its child processes and add up their memory. Now close the app and watch the entries vanish. That small experiment, seeing a program appear and disappear as processes, is the key idea of this whole page. Everything else a task manager shows is a way of measuring those processes: how long they run, what they hold, and what they touch.

title: Why Signed Package Repositories Matter (and What They Don't Protect)
desc: How apt and pacman verify what you install, what a signature does and doesn't prove, and why we publish our own signed repositories.
text: Security Why Signed Package Repositories Matter (and What They Don't Protect) 2026-10-11 · sabaoongfx · 3 min read When you run a command to install software from a repository, you are trusting a long chain: the server, the network between you and it, and the people who built the package. A signature is how that chain is verified. It is a small mechanism with a large effect, and it is worth understanding, especially since Open Task Manager publishes its own signed apt and pacman repositories. What a signature does A publisher holds a private key and shares the matching public key. When they publish a repository, they sign its index (and in pacman’s case, the packages too) with the private key. Your package manager, which has the public key, checks the signature before installing anything. If anyone modified the files after signing, the check fails and the install stops. This protects you against several real risks: Tampering in transit. A hostile network or proxy can't swap in a modified package. A compromised mirror or host. If the server storing the files is hacked, the attacker can replace files but not produce a valid signature without the private key. Silent corruption. Damaged downloads are caught. What it doesn’t do It doesn’t prove the software is safe. A signature says “this came from the key holder,” not “this is harmless.” A signed package from a malicious publisher is still malicious. It doesn’t protect against a stolen key. If the signing key leaks, an attacker can sign anything. This is why keys should be kept in protected storage and rotated if exposed. It doesn’t verify the first key. You must obtain the public key the first time over a channel you trust. If an attacker substitutes the key, they control what verifies. That last point is the weakest link in every system. Check the key fingerprint against a second source, such as the project’s repository, when you add a new repository. How our repositories work Open Task Manager is published through GitHub Pages with one GPG key that signs both the pacman and apt repositories. When a release is published, an automated workflow rebuilds the whole site from scratch, so only the newest version is kept. The pacman package is built from source in an Arch Linux container, signed, and added with repo-add . The apt repository is built with reprepro from the release’s .deb . The apt step waits for the pacman build to succeed, so a failed build leaves the previous site untouched rather than breaking one of the repositories. Prerelease tags are skipped entirely because the Arch version field can’t contain a hyphen. The Arch User Repository packages are prepared but not yet published, because new registrations on the AUR were closed when we set this up. What you should do Prefer signed sources when a project offers them, rather than downloading random installers. Verify the key when you add it. Compare the fingerprint with the one published on the project page. Keep your system updated so you receive fixes, including revoked keys. Remember the limits. Signing guards the delivery, not the contents. That is why open code matters too ( supply chain attacks ). Note that our Windows and macOS installers are not code-signed yet, which is a gap we have listed on the roadmap . Until then, expect a warning when you first open them, and verify downloads from the official release page.

title: Why the Windows Task Manager's CPU Numbers Changed in 24H2
desc: For years the Processes tab and the Performance tab disagreed about CPU usage. Here is why, what Microsoft changed in 2025, and how to read CPU numbers in any tool.
text: How-to Why the Windows Task Manager's CPU Numbers Changed in 24H2 2026-10-11 · sabaoongfx · 3 min read If you ever noticed that the Windows Task Manager showed one CPU percentage for a program on the Processes tab and a different total on the Performance tab, you were not imagining it. The two views used different calculations for years. In 2025, Microsoft changed the Processes tab to match, and the story is a good way to understand what a “CPU percentage” actually is. Two metrics, one label The older Processes tab used a metric called Processor Utility, which was designed to reflect how busy a core is relative to its current frequency and capabilities. The Performance and Users views used a different measure based on the share of time the processor spent working. Because they weren’t the same, a single heavily loaded core on a many-core machine could make the Processes tab look much busier than the overall figure suggested, and a program could even appear to pin the CPU at 100 percent when it wasn’t using it all. What Microsoft did Microsoft first tested a standardised formula in an Insider build in early 2025 and brought it to Windows 11 24H2 with the May 2025 update (KB5058411). The Processes tab now uses the same calculation as the Performance and Users tabs: CPU % = (change in process CPU time) / (elapsed time x logical processors) In plain words: how much processor time the program consumed, divided by how much was available across all logical processors. A program that fully loads one core of an eight-core machine now shows about 12.5 percent, which matches intuition. If you prefer the old figure, you can add the CPU Utility column on the Details tab by right-clicking a column header. Not every tool agrees, either. Community explanations note that the Details tab and Sysinternals’ Process Explorer use Processor Time, which is a different basis. That is a secondary explanation rather than an official statement, but it matches the experience of seeing different numbers in different tools. Reading CPU numbers anywhere The lesson applies to every monitor, including ours. Before trusting a number, ask what it is relative to: Relative to one core. Many Unix-style tools report 100 percent per core, so a busy multi-threaded process can read 400 percent on four cores. Open Task Manager used this convention for individual processes until version 0.4.2, when it moved to the whole-machine share so rows add up to the total, like Windows. Relative to the whole machine. This is the style Microsoft now uses, where 100 percent means every logical processor is saturated. Relative to frequency. Utility-style measures adjust for how fast the core is running at that moment, which can shift numbers on laptops that change speed constantly. Practical advice Compare readings within one tool over time rather than across tools. Check the Performance chart for the overall picture before blaming one process. Watch for sustained load, not spikes. Brief jumps to a high percentage are normal. Remember the number of logical processors; it explains most of the surprise. Our guide to CPU usage in detail goes further, and process versus thread explains why the arithmetic works this way.

title: Why Your Browser Uses So Much Memory, and What You Can Do About It
desc: Multi-process design, site isolation, extensions and tab habits explain the numbers. Here is how to read them and trim them.
text: How-to Why Your Browser Uses So Much Memory, and What You Can Do About It 2026-10-11 · sabaoongfx · 3 min read Open a task manager and the biggest line on your list is almost certainly your web browser. It is such a common sight that people assume something is wrong. Usually nothing is. Browsers are among the most complex programs you run, and the memory they use is largely a deliberate trade for speed, stability and security. Still, there is plenty you can control. Why browsers use many processes Modern browsers split their work across processes: a main browser process, separate processes for web pages, a GPU process, a network service, and one per extension in some designs. The reasons are good ones. A crashing tab shouldn’t take down the others, and keeping sites in separate processes makes it harder for a malicious page to read another page’s data. That isolation costs memory, because each process carries its own copy of some runtime data. What a tab really costs Tabs differ enormously. A static article might need a few dozen megabytes; a web app such as a spreadsheet, video editor or social feed can need hundreds. Pages hold images, scripts, a layout tree and often a large JavaScript heap. Background tabs keep most of that unless the browser discards them. Extensions add their own overhead, and some inject code into every page you visit. A dozen extensions can add more memory than a dozen idle tabs. Reading the numbers correctly Because the browser is many processes, you must look at the total, not one row. Use a grouped Processes view so all helpers add up under the browser’s name. Be aware that resident memory counts shared pages in each process, so the sum can overstate the true cost ( why ). Browsers also include their own task manager, usually under a “more tools” menu, that shows memory per tab and per extension. Use it to find the heavy pages. Ways to reduce it Close tabs you aren’t using. Bookmark or use a reading list instead of keeping 60 pages open as a to-do list. Turn on tab discarding. Most major browsers have an option that unloads inactive tabs and reloads them when you click. Check your browser’s performance settings. Audit extensions. Disable them all, then re-enable only those you need. Remove the rest. Watch for heavy sites. Pages with autoplay video, live feeds and web apps are the biggest. Use the browser’s own task manager to name them. Restart the browser occasionally. Long sessions accumulate memory. Most browsers restore your tabs. Keep it updated. Memory improvements and leak fixes arrive regularly. When high usage is a good thing If you have plenty of free RAM, a browser that caches aggressively is doing you a favour: pages reopen instantly. High memory use only becomes a problem when it crowds out other programs or pushes the system into swapping. Check the Performance chart before you start closing things. If memory is nowhere near full, there is nothing to fix. A note on desktop apps built on browsers Many desktop programs, including chat clients and note-taking tools, are web pages in disguise and carry their own browser engine, so each one is another full browser in memory. That is one reason we built Open Task Manager with Tauri, which uses the web view already on your system instead of bundling a new one. We compare the approaches in Tauri vs. Electron: what the numbers say . For the full set of habits, see our RAM guide .

title: Windows 10 Support Ended. A Task-Manager Guide for Linux Newcomers
desc: Windows 10 reached end of support on October 14, 2025. If you are curious about Linux, here is how to find what you are used to finding.
text: Linux Windows 10 Support Ended. A Task-Manager Guide for Linux Newcomers 2026-10-11 · sabaoongfx · 3 min read Microsoft ended support for Windows 10 on October 14, 2025. Machines that can’t run Windows 11 stopped getting free security updates, and that pushed a lot of people to ask whether Linux could be the answer. If you are one of them, the first week is mostly about finding the familiar things in unfamiliar places. A task manager is a good place to start, because it answers the question you will ask most often: “why is my computer slow right now?” Is everyone really switching? Not in the numbers, and it is worth being skeptical of big claims. Steam’s October 2025 survey showed Linux crossing 3 percent of Steam users for the first time (3.05 percent), and the November survey put it at 3.2 percent, ahead of macOS on that platform. StatCounter’s all-desktop figures for the United States showed Linux at 3.49 percent in October 2025 after a brief spike above 5 percent in June. Two caveats apply. Steam’s sample is gamers, who skew technical, and a large part of Linux’s Steam share is Steam Deck hardware. And reporting suggests that most people leaving Windows 10 moved to Windows 11, not to Linux. So Linux is growing, but slowly, and mostly among people who chose it on purpose. If you are trying it, you are still in a small group. Where things live: Windows to Linux On Windows On Linux Task Manager (Ctrl+Shift+Esc) A system monitor app from your distribution, or Open Task Manager End task Kill or terminate a process (see ending a stuck process ) Services app systemd services ( explained here ) Startup apps Autostart entries in your desktop settings Resource Monitor The Performance tab, or a terminal tool such as htop or otm C: drive One file tree starting at / ; your files live in /home/yourname Your first-week checklist Install a monitor you recognise. Open Task Manager keeps the Windows 11 layout, so the Processes, Performance, Startup apps and Users tabs are where you expect them. On Ubuntu, Debian, Mint and Pop!_OS it installs from a signed apt repository. Look at the Processes tab with nothing open. This is your baseline. Note total memory used at idle so you can tell later what changed. Open your usual apps and watch. Your browser will probably be the biggest item, as it was on Windows. Check Startup apps. A fresh install may launch things you don’t need at login. Learn one terminal tool. You will meet SSH and servers eventually, and a text-mode monitor works over both. We compare the options . Things that will look odd Memory shows as used even when little is running. Linux uses spare RAM as disk cache and gives it back when needed, so “used” is not the same as “in trouble.” You will see processes you don’t recognise. Most are small desktop helpers. Search the name before ending anything. Some actions need administrator rights. Ending another user’s process, or a system one, will be refused unless you elevate. The point isn’t that Linux is better or worse than Windows. It is that the basic skill of reading what your machine is doing carries over, and a familiar-looking tool makes the move less jarring.

title: Windows Recall and the Case for Software You Can Audit
desc: Recall's 2024 launch became a lesson in how trust works for software that watches what you do. What changed, and what 'auditable' really gives you.
text: Privacy Windows Recall and the Case for Software You Can Audit 2026-10-11 · sabaoongfx · 3 min read When Microsoft first showed Windows Recall in 2024, the idea was simple: the computer takes a snapshot of your screen every few seconds so you can search your own history later. The reaction was not. Security researchers pointed out that anyone who got into your machine for even a moment could read a detailed record of everything you had done, and that early versions stored much of that data in plain text. Within weeks Microsoft changed course. What changed after the backlash Reporting at the time says Microsoft made Recall opt-in rather than on by default, required Windows Hello to access it, and added stronger encryption to the stored data. The company has said the data stays on the device. The UK’s Information Commissioner’s Office said it was talking with Microsoft about data protection. The current state of the feature is for Microsoft’s own documentation to say; we are describing the original controversy, not auditing today’s version, and you should check before relying on any of it. The episode is useful whatever you think of Recall itself, because it shows how the trust problem works. The trust problem with closed software When a program is closed source, you trust three things at once: that the vendor describes it honestly, that the vendor builds it correctly, and that the vendor won’t change it later. Each is reasonable, and each is a promise rather than something you can check. Recall’s plain-text storage was caught by outside researchers who examined the running software, not because anyone could read the code. Open source doesn’t remove the need for trust, but it changes what it rests on. Anyone can read the code, build it, and compare it with what is distributed. A change that added tracking would appear in the public history. That is verifiability, not virtue: an open project can still be careless, but its behaviour is checkable by people with no reason to take the author’s word. What “local-first” means Local-first software keeps your data on your device and treats any network use as optional rather than required. A useful test has three questions: Where does the data live? On your disk, in a format you can inspect, or on someone else’s server? What does it do without a network? If the answer is “nothing,” the product depends on a server. What would a skeptic find? If someone watched its network traffic for an hour, what would they see? For a system monitor, the right answers are boring on purpose. It reads from your operating system, draws a window, and stores nothing. Open Task Manager’s own comparison with the built-in tool goes into this in detail: Open Task Manager vs. the Windows Task Manager . Practical steps Prefer tools whose source is public and whose releases can be matched to it. Check what any app sends, using the method in how to check what an app sends over the network . Review the privacy toggles in your operating system after major updates ( Windows guide ). Be most careful with software that records your activity, because the cost of a mistake is highest there. The lesson from Recall isn’t that one company got it wrong. It is that software that sees everything should earn trust by being checkable, and that the checking should not depend on goodwill.

title: Zombie and Orphan Processes on Linux: What They Are and What to Do
desc: Why you can't kill a zombie, why it usually doesn't matter, and the one situation where it does.
text: Linux Zombie and Orphan Processes on Linux: What They Are and What to Do 2026-10-11 · sabaoongfx · 3 min read Sooner or later a Linux user sees a process marked Z or labelled “defunct” and tries to kill it. Nothing happens, however many times they try. That isn’t a bug, and understanding why also explains how processes live and die on Unix-like systems. How a process ends When a process exits, the kernel frees almost everything it held: its memory, its open files, its CPU time. But it keeps one small record, the process’s exit status, until the parent process reads it. That reading is done with a system call named wait . It exists so a parent can learn whether a child succeeded or failed. What a zombie is A zombie is a process that has finished running but whose parent hasn’t yet read its exit status. It is dead, but its entry stays in the process table. It uses no CPU and (essentially) no memory. The only thing it occupies is a slot, and one process ID. This is why you can’t kill it: it’s already dead. Sending signals to it does nothing because there is no running code to receive them. The entry vanishes when the parent finally calls wait , or when the parent itself exits. Are zombies a problem? Usually not. A few that appear briefly are completely normal. You should care only in two cases: They pile up. A buggy parent that keeps spawning children and never collects them can accumulate thousands, eventually exhausting the available process IDs and blocking new processes from starting. They persist. A zombie that stays for hours points to a parent that is stuck or misbehaving. What to do about them Find the parent. In a terminal, ps -o pid,ppid,stat,cmd shows each process’s parent ID. Tools with a tree view, such as htop , make the relationship visible ( our comparison ). Ask the parent to behave. Some parents collect children when they receive the SIGCHLD signal. Restart the parent. If the parent is a stuck service, restarting it clears its zombies ( services explained ). Report the bug. If it recurs, the program is failing to reap its children. Do not kill the parent if it is something critical, such as your session manager or a database, just to remove a zombie. The cure is worse than the condition. Orphans are different An orphan is a process that is still running after its parent has exited. Linux handles this automatically: orphaned processes are adopted by the init process (PID 1, usually systemd), which collects them when they end. Orphans are often deliberate. A background service started from a terminal and left running is an orphan, and that’s fine. They are only a concern if you didn’t intend them to keep running; in that case, find them in the process list and end them ( safely ). In Open Task Manager The Details tab lists processes with their status, so zombies show up there if the operating system reports them. We don't yet show parent-child relationships, which is where the tree view in htop is stronger. If you are learning how processes relate, the Details tab together with our beginner’s guide is a good start.
